blocks.html: Although this proof was not very cogent [neceſſaire: compelling], because a testimony of having heard say [hearsay] proves nothing a2; nevertheless when the true Martin Guerre arrived in such equipage, namely having a wooden leg, and bearing an attestation of having lost the foot from a cannon-shot before Saint-Quentin, the Judges began to be spurred by a sharp goad to enter into some suspicion of the imposture.

notes.citation: Decretals, X 2.20.33 (De testibus et attestationibus, c. Tam litteris; the print's iam literis) and X 2.20.47 (c. Licet ex quadam, Innocent III, on witnesses who depose from hearsay); X 4.14.7 (De consanguinitate et affinitate, c. Tua nos: hearsay testimony on degrees of kinship minus est validum; the print's rutela, which the parallel note at annot-052 {c} prints tua)
notes.original: c. iam literis. c, licet ex quadam, deſti. c. rutela. de. conſan. & affini,
notes.gloss: Deſti. is the print's contraction for de teſti[bus]; rutela is a wrong sort for tua (c. Tua nos). Cited for the rule that testimony de auditu makes no proof.
